Case A

A1. The seven-day search was requested from 7 days before publication but evaluated only from 2 hours before publication, and its status is partial. Earlier requests outside that window were not checked, so "only those" does not cover the full period. The 19-minute burst may not have been the first misuse, and the records cannot settle it. Answer: Cannot tell.

A2. The compromise check scored 30 minutes after publication using inputs as of that time. The link between the new payout destination and two other accounts was effective before publication but was learned only 1 day after. It was not available to the check when it scored. Answer: No.

A3. A shared payout destination does not by itself show one owner. Answer: No, not by itself.

A4. Neither outcome channel has a reporting window defined, so the absence of reports after 30 days cannot be read as evidence of legitimacy. Answer: Cannot tell. The option "No" could also be argued, but "Cannot tell" fits better because the channels may simply not have been able to register anything. I chose Cannot tell.

A5. The burst used a different fingerprint through a residential proxy and changed the payout destination and schedule, so it warrants investigation. Answer: Yes.

Case B

B1. Recorded chargebacks at D are 0, but 2 chargebacks recorded at account X are linked to D's transactions. D's true count is therefore 2, the same as the others in the counts (A 2, B 2, C 2). D is not lower. Answer: No.

B2. The combined 5 percent is an aggregate. The per-account measure shows A at 8 of 100 and B at 8 of 100, both above 5 percent. Answer: No.

B3. The search was partial and truncated, with one source sampled at 10 percent and the row limit reached. It cannot show that no other accounts exist. Answer: Cannot tell.

B4. Both notes link to the agent's cluster assessment, which was open in the case when each note was written. They are not independent. Answer: No.

B5. The block decision closed the chargeback channel for that payment, so the lack of a chargeback says nothing about whether it was fraud. Answer: No.

B6. Shared templates and a descriptor pattern, plus a person linked to A, a closed account and a rejected application, justify a joint investigation. Answer: Yes. The option list is "Yes / No / Cannot tell", so I answer Yes.

RESULT CN-069 | A1: Cannot tell | A2: No | A3: No, not by itself | A4: Cannot tell | A5: Yes | B1: No | B2: No | B3: Cannot tell | B4: No | B5: No | B6: Yes
